Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use breast-cancer.csv, which contains 569 cases from the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset. Predict y (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using mean_radius, mean_texture, and mean_smoothness.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{5,15,25,35,45}. k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.

Using the estimated probabilities for y = 1 on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

Solution

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

# Read data
df = pd.read_csv("data/breast-cancer.csv")

X = df[["mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness"]]
y = df["y"]

# 70/30 train-test split
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.30,
    random_state=432
)

# Standardize using TRAINING data only
scaler = StandardScaler()

X_train_std = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_std = scaler.transform(X_test)

# Store predicted probabilities
predictions = {}

# Logistic regression: intercept, no penalty
logistic = LogisticRegression(
    penalty=None,
    max_iter=10000
)

logistic.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

predictions["Logistic"] = logistic.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]

# KNN
for k in [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]:

    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        weights="uniform",
        metric="euclidean"
    )

    knn.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

    predictions[f"KNN k={k}"] = knn.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))

auc_values = {}

for name, probs in predictions.items():

    fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_test, probs)

    auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, probs)
    auc_values[name] = auc

    plt.plot(
        fpr,
        tpr,
        label=f"{name}: AUC = {auc:.3f}"
    )

# Random classifier reference
plt.plot(
    [0, 1],
    [0, 1],
    linestyle="--"
)

plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.title("ROC Curves: Logistic Regression vs KNN")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

for name, auc in auc_values.items():
    print(f"{name}: {auc:.3f}")

Use l1_ratio=0 instead of penalty='l2', l1_ratio=1 instead of penalty='l1', l1_ratio set to a float between 0 and 1 instead of penalty='elasticnet', and C=np.inf instead of penalty=None.

Logistic: 0.982
KNN k=5: 0.956
KNN k=15: 0.970
KNN k=25: 0.978
KNN k=35: 0.978
KNN k=45: 0.978

I prefer logistic regression because it has the highest test AUC among the six fitted models. The KNN models with larger values of kk perform very similarly to logistic regression, so the difference is small. However, based on the test AUC, logistic regression provides the best discrimination between malignant and benign cases on this test set.

Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{1,3,5,10,20}. k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its kk nearest neighbors.

For each kk, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with kk. In particular, explain what happens at k=1k=1 and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

Solution

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

k_values = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(20, 4))

for ax, k in zip(axes, k_values):

    # Fit KNN
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        weights="uniform",
        metric="euclidean"
    )

    knn.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

    # Predicted probabilities
    train_probs = knn.predict_proba(X_train_std)[:, 1]
    test_probs = knn.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]

    # ROC curves
    train_fpr, train_tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_train, train_probs)
    test_fpr, test_tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, test_probs)

    # AUC
    train_auc = roc_auc_score(y_train, train_probs)
    test_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probs)

    # Plot
    ax.plot(
        train_fpr,
        train_tpr,
        label=f"Train AUC = {train_auc:.3f}"
    )

    ax.plot(
        test_fpr,
        test_tpr,
        label=f"Test AUC = {test_auc:.3f}"
    )

    ax.plot(
        [0, 1],
        [0, 1],
        linestyle="--"
    )

    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}")
    ax.set_xlabel("False Positive Rate")
    ax.set_ylabel("True Positive Rate")
    ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Training performance is better than test performance for small values of kk, and the gap decreases as kk increases. At k=1k=1, each training observation is its own nearest neighbor, so the training AUC is 1. However, the test performance is much worse, indicating overfitting.

As kk increases, the model becomes smoother and less flexible. The training AUC decreases slightly, while the test AUC improves. By k=20k=20, the training and test ROC curves are very similar, suggesting better generalization. This pattern reflects the bias–variance tradeoff: small kk has low bias and high variance, while larger kk reduces variance but increases bias.
